reason: The proof first identifies the unique possible limit and then directly negates uniform convergence using the fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon=1/2\).
text:
For each \(x\in[0,1)\), we have \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Any uniform limit would also be the pointwise limit, so it suffices to show that \(f_n\not\to f\) uniformly. Fix \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), choose \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\in[0,1)\). Then \(f(x)=0\) and
\[
|f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Hence, for every \(N\), there are \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\). This contradicts the criterion for uniform convergence. Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).
